title: South Carolina Fine Print: State Law
description: South Carolina law that parents rarely hear about: autism insurance coverage and its limits, coverage past the age limit, and school rights at 18.
summary: South Carolina autism insurance law and its limits, coverage past the age limit, rights at 18, and mediation.
short_answer: South Carolina law requires covered group health plans to cover autism treatment (for children diagnosed by age 8 and under 16, with a yearly behavioral therapy cap), can stretch dependent coverage past the age limit for a child who cannot support themselves, moves school rights to the student at 18 with ways to delegate or designate a representative, and requires free mediation that does not give up due process.
h1: South Carolina Fine Print: What State Law Adds
intro: This page is about South Carolina only. Roy lived all of this here, and the federal rules cover the whole country, but states add their own layer on top. These are the South Carolina laws that most parents never hear about, each with the exact sentence from the state code.

sections.html:
South Carolina has a state insurance law that requires health plans to cover autism treatment. It is real and it is useful, and it also has edges that catch families by surprise.

The law says: “A health insurance plan as defined in this section must provide coverage for the treatment of autism spectrum disorder.” (S.C. Code 38-71-280(B))

Coverage is tied to a treatment plan from the child's treating medical doctor, and the plan cannot hold autism coverage to worse dollar limits, deductibles or coinsurance than it applies to physical illness in general.

The law says: “The coverage required pursuant to subsection (B) must not be subject to dollar limits, deductibles, or coinsurance provisions that are less favorable to an insured than the dollar limits, deductibles, or coinsurance provisions that apply to physical illness generally under the health insurance plan” (S.C. Code 38-71-280(C))

Now the edges. The law has an age and diagnosis rule and a dollar cap for behavioral therapy.

The law says: “To be eligible for benefits and coverage under this section, an individual must be diagnosed with autistic spectrum disorder at age eight or younger. The benefits and coverage provided pursuant to this section must be provided to any eligible person under sixteen years of age. Coverage for behavioral therapy is subject to a fifty thousand dollar maximum benefit per year.” (S.C. Code 38-71-280(E))

The cap is adjusted each January, so ask what this year's number is. And not every plan is covered. The definition of a covered plan leaves some out.

The law says: “It includes the State Health Plan, but does not otherwise include any health insurance plan offered in the individual market as defined in Section 38-71-670(11), any health insurance plan that is individually underwritten, or any health insurance plan provided to a small employer, as defined by Section 38-71-1330(17).” (S.C. Code 38-71-280(A))

So the first question is which kind of plan you have. Also, the plan may ask for an updated treatment plan, but only on a schedule.

The law says: “The health insurance plan may only request an updated treatment plan once every six months from the treating medical doctor to review medical necessity” (S.C. Code 38-71-280(D))

Say: “Is our plan a group plan covered by South Carolina's autism coverage law (38-71-280)? What is this year's behavioral therapy maximum, and what do you need from the treating doctor?”

sections.h2: A Child Who Cannot Support Themselves Can Stay on the Plan Past the Age Limit
sections.html:
Many families treat the end of dependent coverage as a hard stop. South Carolina has a rule that can stretch it for a child with a disability who is still dependent on the parent.

The law says: “attainment of the limiting age does not operate to terminate the coverage of the child while the child is and continues to be both (a) incapable of self-sustaining employment by reason of intellectual disability or physical handicap and (b) chiefly dependent upon the policyholder or subscriber for support and maintenance” (S.C. Code 38-71-350)

Read the lead-in of the section carefully. It names individual hospital or medical expense insurance policies and hospital or medical service plan contracts delivered or issued in South Carolina. An employer's plan may be governed by different rules, so ask in writing which law applies. Plans also differ in what proof they need and by when, so ask early. Roy's Ages 14 to 26 page is where the 26 warning comes from, and the Turning 18 and 26 fine print covers the federal rule.

Say: “My adult child is dependent on me and cannot support themselves because of a disability. Does this policy continue coverage past the age limit under South Carolina Code 38-71-350, what proof do you need, and what is the deadline?”

sections.h2: At 18, School Rights Move to the Student Automatically
sections.html:
The federal rule lets each state decide whether school rights move to the young person at the age of majority. South Carolina has decided that they do.

The law says: “all rights accorded to the student's parents under this article transfer to the student except as provided in Sections 59-33-330 and 59-33-340” (S.C. Code 59-33-320)

The exceptions are the useful part. The student can hand decision-making to another adult.

The law says: “An adult student may delegate educational rights by naming an agent through a duly executed power of attorney or by using a form that the State Department of Education shall develop and provide.” (S.C. Code 59-33-330)

And when a student cannot communicate their wishes about their education, even with accommodations, a process lets a representative be designated. It can start earlier than most families realize.

The law says: “as early as sixty calendar days before his eighteenth birthday” (S.C. Code 59-33-340)

The law sets the steps, including a written certification from a professional, so ask the school district for the form and the procedure well before the birthday. Guardianship is a larger step with other paths around it, and a South Carolina attorney who handles special needs planning can explain what fits your family.

Say: “My child turns 18 on this date. What is the process in this district to delegate educational decisions or to designate an educational representative under South Carolina Code 59-33-330 and 59-33-340, and what form do you use?”

sections.h2: Mediation Does Not Cost You Your Hearing
sections.html:
If you and the school disagree, South Carolina requires a free mediation process, and the law says clearly that choosing it does not give up your other rights.

The law says: “it must be clearly stated that the right of the parents or the school district to due process is in no way compromised by agreeing to mediation and that neither parents nor the school district are bound by the outcomes of mediation” (S.C. Code 59-33-110)

It is a good first step when the relationship matters. The disagree-in-writing guide shows the order of steps.

sections.h2: What Counts as Special Education Services in South Carolina
sections.html:
The state's definition of special education services is broader than a classroom. It reaches into things like transportation and therapy.

The law says: “"Special education services" shall mean, but not be limited to, special classes, special housing, homebound instruction, special rental facilities” (S.C. Code 59-33-20(c))

The list goes on to include braille services for students who are blind or visually impaired, and the items parents ask about most:

The law says: “transportation, maintenance, instructional materials, therapy, professional consultant services, psychological services, itinerant services and resource services” (S.C. Code 59-33-20(c))

If your child needs one of these to benefit from school, ask for it at the IEP meeting and ask for it to be written into the IEP.

sections.h2: DDSN Services Do Not Reduce Your Rights as a Parent
sections.html:
Some parents worry that signing up with the state disability agency means giving up a say. The law says no.

The law says: “Admission to services of the Office of Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities does not terminate or reduce the rights and responsibilities of parents.” (S.C. Code 44-20-20)

It also says that being in a DDSN program does not close the door on regular public school classes.

The law says: “does not preclude his attendance in community-based public school classes when the individual qualifies for the classes” (S.C. Code 44-20-510)

sections.h2: A Way to Ask That Works
sections.html: These are state rules, so they are the same wherever you live in South Carolina, and they come with their own forms and offices. Ask in writing, keep a copy, and thank the person who helps. Your South Carolina parent center, Family Connection of South Carolina, can check how a rule applies to your situation for free. The Your State page links to the official rights notices.

checked: Every quoted sentence on this page was checked, word for word, against the text of the South Carolina Code of Laws (S.C. Code 38-71-280, 38-71-350, 44-20-20, 44-20-510, 59-33-20, 59-33-110, 59-33-320, 59-33-330 and 59-33-340) at scstatehouse.gov. Laws change, and a plan or district may apply them in ways this page does not cover.
